dataset.what_one_row_represents: One FAERS safety report (faers_2024_sample.csv). Each report explodes into one row per drug (faers_2024_drugs.csv) and one row per reaction (faers_2024_reactions.csv).
dataset.time_range_observed: 2024-01-01 to 2024-02-23 (54 unique receivedates; the 200,000-report cap was reached after roughly 7 weeks of 2024)
dataset.geographic_scope: Global; 68.4% of reports filed FROM the US, 60.3% of events OCCUR in the US

ana_01.label: Three linked tables, ~1.57 million rows in total
ana_01.content: The dataset is three CSV files joined by safetyreportid. faers_2024_sample.csv has 200,000 rows (one per report) and 14 columns; faers_2024_drugs.csv has 776,793 rows (one per drug-report pairing) and 7 columns; faers_2024_reactions.csv has 597,802 rows (one per reaction-report pairing) and 4 columns. The average report touches 3.88 drugs and 2.99 reactions; the median report mentions 2 drugs and 2 reactions. The maximum number of drugs in a single report is 1,384, which corresponds to a polypharmacy / clinical-trial protocol case.

calculation.output:
sample: rows=200,000 cols=14
drugs: rows=776,793 cols=7
reactions: rows=597,802 cols=4

data_table.description: Row counts across the three FAERS 2024 tables

ana_02.label: The 200,000-report cap was hit after 54 days
ana_02.content: Although the README describes the data as a 2024 sample, the receivedate field shows the API actually delivered the first 200,000 chronologically-ordered reports of the year: January 1, 2024 through February 23, 2024. That is 54 distinct dates out of 366 calendar days. The full FAERS 2024 universe contains roughly 1.32 million reports, so this slice is approximately 15% of the year — proportionally representative of the early-2024 reporting pattern but not of seasonal or late-year trends.

ana_03.label: Missing-data profile of the summary table
ana_03.content: Of the 14 columns in the summary file, the patient demographic columns are missing the most often. Patient age is missing for 40.2% of reports, patient sex is missing for 15.9%, and occur-country is missing for 10.8%. The seriousness sub-flags (death, hospitalization) are missing for only 3–4%, and the master `serious` flag is essentially complete (6 missing out of 200,000). This pattern matches FAERS reporting norms: reporters reliably tell FDA whether the event was serious, but consumer- and pharmacist-filed reports often omit the patient's age and sex.

calculation.output:
patient_onset_age: 80,430 (40.2%)
patient_sex: 31,830 (15.9%)
occurcountry: 21,565 (10.8%)
seriousnessdeath: 8,211 (4.1%)
seriousnesshospitalization: 6,238 (3.1%)
primarysourcecountry: 1,114 (0.6%)
serious: 6 (0.0%)

data_table.description: Missingness per column in the 200k summary file

ana_04.label: Encoding correction: '2' means 'no', not 'blank'
ana_04.content: The README says seriousnessdeath and seriousnesshospitalization are coded 1=true and blank=false. The actual data encodes them as 1=true, 2=false, and NaN=missing. seriousnessdeath has 18,865 ones (9.4%), 172,924 twos (86.5%), and 8,211 missing values. Without correcting this, every chart that filters on `seriousnessdeath != null` would overcount deaths fourteen-fold. Every seriousness statistic in this analysis uses the value 1 as the positive class.

calculation.output:
seriousnessdeath: 1.0=18,865  2.0=172,924  NaN=8,211
seriousnesshospitalization: 1.0=38,124  2.0=155,638  NaN=6,238

ana_05.label: Half of reports mention just 1–2 drugs, but the tail is enormous
ana_05.content: The number of drugs per report is highly skewed. 49% of reports mention exactly one drug, and 66% mention at most two. The 75th percentile is 3 drugs, but the mean is 3.88 because of a long tail: 9,036 reports mention 11 or more drugs, and the heaviest report names 1,384. These long-tail reports are almost always polypharmacy cases — oncology trial protocols, transplant immunosuppression cocktails, or geriatric patients with many concomitant prescriptions. Reactions follow a similar shape: median 2, mean 2.99, max 200.

data_table.description: Number of distinct drugs mentioned in a report

ana_06.label: Dupixent and Mounjaro tie for #1 among all named drugs
ana_06.content: Of 776,793 drug rows, the most-reported product is Dupixent (dupilumab — an injectable biologic for atopic dermatitis and asthma) with 15,027 mentions, exactly 1.93% of the dataset. Mounjaro (tirzepatide for type-2 diabetes) is a near-tie at 14,908 mentions (1.92%). The two are followed by Xolair (omalizumab for asthma) at 8,720 mentions and the workhorse cancer-clinic combo of methotrexate, prednisone, Repatha, and Cabometyx. Ozempic — the GLP-1 drug at the center of the 2024 weight-loss story — ranks twenty-first with 3,593 mentions; its sibling Zepbound, launched in November 2023, is right behind at 3,077. The headline story of the 2024 dataset is that Dupixent and the tirzepatide brands have crowded out the older immunology and oncology blockbusters that historically dominated FAERS.

data_table.description: Top 25 most-reported drugs by any role (drug rows)

notable_instance.name: Dupixent vs Mounjaro
notable_instance.value: 15,027 vs 14,908 — a difference of 119 mentions across 776,793 rows
notable_instance.why: The closeness undercuts the press narrative that GLP-1 drugs dominate FAERS; in this 2024 slice, Dupixent is essentially tied with Mounjaro for the top spot.

ana_07.label: Suspect-role ranking: same leaders, sharper signal
ana_07.content: When the analysis is restricted to drugs marked as the *suspect* product (drugcharacterization = 1, meaning the reporter believes this drug caused the event), the field tightens and the ranking sharpens. Dupixent (14,916 suspect rows, 3.01% of all suspect-drug rows) is still #1 by a hair over Mounjaro (14,742, 2.98%). Acetaminophen drops from #8 to #21 because it is most often mentioned as a concomitant medication, not as the suspect. Aspirin disappears from the top 25 entirely. The suspect ranking is the more meaningful surveillance signal: it is roughly what FDA looks at when prioritizing safety signals.

data_table.description: Top 25 drugs by suspect-role appearances (drugcharacterization = 1)

ana_08.label: Aspirin and acetaminophen are mostly bystanders, not suspects
ana_08.content: Drugs split sharply on whether they appear as the suspect or merely as concomitant medication. Dupixent (99.3% suspect), Mounjaro (98.9%), Xolair (99.1%), Repatha (99.0%), and Cabometyx (99.8%) are almost never reported as bystanders — when they show up, they are the drug under suspicion. By contrast, aspirin is the suspect in only 15.8% of its mentions (the other 83.0% are concomitant), and acetaminophen is 50/50. This is exactly what you would expect: people on cancer therapy or biologics are also on a daily aspirin or acetaminophen, but the reporter rarely blames the painkiller for an adverse event. The role mix is a useful diagnostic for whether a drug's headline count reflects a real safety signal or simply how common the prescription is.

DUPIXENT: 99.26% suspect, 0.71% concom
MOUNJARO: 98.89% suspect, 1.05% concom
ACETAMINOPHEN: 48.95% suspect, 49.57% concom
ASPIRIN: 15.85% suspect, 83.05% concom
ATORVASTATIN: 21.69% suspect, 78.07% concom
GABAPENTIN: 34.15% suspect, 65.19% concom

data_table.description: Suspect / Concomitant / Interacting role mix for the top 12 most-reported drugs

ana_09.label: Tirzepatide outruns semaglutide 3.3 to 1 inside the GLP-1 class
ana_09.content: Pooled across all brand names, GLP-1 receptor agonists account for 26,170 drug rows — 3.37% of all drug appearances in the dataset. Within that class, tirzepatide (Mounjaro + Zepbound) is the dominant contributor at 18,035 rows, three-and-a-third times the 5,425 rows for semaglutide (Ozempic + Wegovy + Rybelsus). Dulaglutide (Trulicity) is third at 2,060, followed by liraglutide (Victoza + Saxenda) at 455 and exenatide (Byetta + Bydureon) at just 195. The 10,056 unique reports involving any GLP-1 drug make up 5.03% of all FAERS reports in the sample. The Mounjaro/Zepbound surge confirms — at the 2024 sampling moment — the press narrative that tirzepatide is generating disproportionately more reports than the older semaglutide products, despite a much shorter time on the market.

ana_12.label: The top 'reaction' isn't medical — it's 'Off label use'
ana_12.content: Of 597,802 reaction rows, the single most common MedDRA Preferred Term is 'Off label use' (14,801 mentions, 2.48%), followed by 'Drug ineffective' (11,335, 1.90%) and 'Death' (9,356, 1.57%). Only at rank four does a recognisably medical symptom appear: 'Fatigue' (8,170, 1.37%). The top ten is heavy with terms that describe how the drug was used or whether it worked, not what happened to the patient: 'Off label use', 'Drug ineffective', 'Product dose omission issue', 'Drug dose omission by device'. This is structural: FAERS reports are filed by anyone who notices a problem, and many manufacturer-mandated reports are triggered by complaints that a drug failed to work or was used outside its label — not by a physical adverse event.

ana_13.label: The reaction long tail: 9,870 distinct terms, top 10 cover only 13.5%
ana_13.content: The MedDRA Preferred Term column contains 9,870 distinct values across 597,802 rows. Concentration is shallow: the top 10 terms cover only 13.5% of all reaction rows, the top 50 cover 33.2%, and you need the top 500 terms to cover three-quarters of all reactions. By contrast, an analysis like the top 25 drugs covers 17.3% of all drug rows. This means reactions cannot be summarised as 'these ten things keep happening' — they form a very long tail, with most rare reactions appearing fewer than 100 times in 200,000 reports.

data_table.description: Cumulative share of reaction rows covered by the top-N MedDRA Preferred Terms

ana_14.label: More than half of reactions end with 'Unknown' outcome
ana_14.content: The reactionoutcome field is filled with 'Unknown' (code 6) in 54.1% of rows. Reports describing reactions that fully resolved (code 1) make up 13.5%; reactions still resolving (code 2) are 6.8%; reactions not resolved (code 3) are 14.2%. Fatal outcomes (code 5) are 6.6%. The 'Unknown' dominance reflects the structural reality of FAERS: most reports are filed soon after the event, the reporter never receives medical follow-up, and the outcome field is never updated. Drug-safety researchers therefore typically treat the Unknown category as 'no information' rather than as a status.

data_table.description: Reaction outcome at last observation

ana_15.label: 1.8% of reports are just someone complaining the drug didn't work
ana_15.content: 11,237 reports (5.6% of all reports) contain 'Drug ineffective' as one of the reactions. In 3,554 of those (1.8% of the entire dataset, or 32% of all 'Drug ineffective' reports), 'Drug ineffective' is the *only* reaction listed — the entire report is one complaint that the drug failed to do what it was supposed to do, with no other adverse event mentioned. These reports are sometimes treated as noise in pharmacovigilance, but the FDA does monitor them because clusters of efficacy-failure reports can signal counterfeit lots, manufacturing problems, or expiry-date issues.

calculation.output:
reports containing 'Drug ineffective': 11,237 of 200,000 (5.62%)
reports where 'Drug ineffective' is ONLY reaction: 3,554 (1.78%)

ana_16.label: What people die of in FAERS: cardiac arrest, suicide, sepsis
ana_16.content: Within the 39,213 reaction rows tagged with the Fatal outcome code, the MedDRA term 'Death' itself accounts for 21.6% — meaning many reports list 'Death' as both the reaction and the outcome rather than naming a specific cause. 'Completed suicide' is the most common identifiable cause at 4.1% (1,602 fatal rows), followed by 'Toxicity to various agents' (2.7%), 'Drug abuse' (2.2%), 'Cardio-respiratory arrest' (1.2%), 'Pneumonia' (0.9%), and 'Cardiac arrest' (0.8%). Notably, 'Drug ineffective' itself appears 304 times with a fatal outcome — these are cases where a drug failed to prevent a fatal outcome it was prescribed to treat (e.g. cancer therapy in metastatic disease).

Death: 8,470 (21.60%)

Toxicity to various agents: 1,059 (2.70%)
Drug abuse: 861 (2.20%)

ana_18.label: 52% of reports are tagged 'serious'; 9% record a death
ana_18.content: The serious flag is on in 104,896 of 200,000 reports (52.5%). Of those, 18,865 reports (9.4% of all 200,000) carry the seriousnessdeath sub-flag, and 38,124 (19.1%) carry the seriousnesshospitalization sub-flag. The 'serious' rate is much higher than naive expectation because serious events are far more likely to be reported in the first place — a mild headache rarely makes it into FAERS, but a hospitalization almost always does. The 9.4% death rate is therefore not 'how often this drug kills' but 'what share of reports involve a death'.

calculation.output:
serious=1: 104,896 (52.45%)
seriousnessdeath=1: 18,865 (9.43%)
seriousnesshospitalization=1: 38,124 (19.06%)
death OR hospitalization: 52,810

data_table.description: Seriousness counts across the 200,000-report sample

ana_19.label: Top-drug seriousness profile: from Inflectra at 99% to Zepbound at 2.5%
ana_19.content: Among the top 20 most-reported drugs, the share of reports tagged serious varies from 98.8% (Inflectra, an infliximab biosimilar used in IBD) down to 2.5% (Zepbound, tirzepatide for obesity). The oncology and immunology blockbusters — Inflectra, Acetaminophen-in-overdose contexts, Vedolizumab, Sulfasalazine, Dexamethasone — all cluster above 95% serious. Mounjaro at 11.0% serious looks remarkably mild compared to Ozempic at 32.0% serious, despite covering similar therapeutic territory. The 'serious' rate per drug is much more about which reporter community is filing reports than about the drug itself: the oncology drugs are mostly reported by hospitals on hospitalised patients, while Zepbound is mostly reported by consumers on outpatient weight-loss regimens.

ana_20.label: The death-rate hotspots are overdose drugs, not weight-loss drugs
ana_20.content: Restricting to drugs with at least 200 suspect-reports, the highest death rates belong to drugs primarily implicated in overdose: methamphetamine (93.5% of its suspect-reports involve a death), alcohol (89.4%), fentanyl (71.9%), diphenhydramine (70.9%), trazodone (69.1%), cocaine (66.1%), and oxycodone (57.9%). These are not signals that the drugs are killing properly-prescribed patients — they are reports filed because someone died with that substance present. Alendronic acid (Fosamax) appears in this group too, but for a different reason: it is reported in atypical-fracture and osteonecrosis cases that have high mortality among elderly patients. Notably absent from the top-30 death-rate list: any GLP-1 drug.

ana_22.label: FAERS reports skew strongly female: 1.47 women per man
ana_22.content: Among reports with a known patient sex, 99,513 (59.5% of sex-known) are female and 67,785 (40.5%) are male — a 1.47:1 ratio. Including the 15.9% of reports with missing sex and the 0.4% explicitly coded Unknown, the absolute counts are: 49.8% female, 33.9% male, 0.4% unknown, 15.9% missing. The female skew is consistent with decades of pharmacovigilance literature: women are prescribed more drugs on average, are more likely to report symptoms to clinicians, and are over-represented in the conditions whose drugs file the most reports (autoimmune disease, depression, osteoporosis, weight-loss). It is also a known source of bias — the FAERS picture of any given drug is colored by who is filing reports about it, not just who is taking it.

data_table.description: Patient sex distribution across the 200,000 reports

ana_23.label: Median patient age is 60; the 50–79 band carries the most reports
ana_23.content: Among the 115,807 reports (57.9%) with a usable age in years, the median is 60 and the mean 55.6. Distribution by age band: under 18 = 6.3%, 18–29 = 7.1%, 30–39 = 9.2%, 40–49 = 11.1%, 50–59 = 16.1%, 60–69 = 21.0%, 70–79 = 19.4%, 80–89 = 8.5%, 90+ = 1.3%. The peak band is 60–69, and 56.5% of reports fall between ages 50 and 79. This matches the prescription-volume reality: older patients take more drugs and have more comorbidities. The 40% missing-age rate (see ana_03) means age-stratified analyses should be treated as descriptive rather than representative.

data_table.description: Age-band distribution of patients with a known age in years

ana_25.label: Where the events happened: US 60%, then Canada, UK, Japan, France
ana_25.content: Of the 178,435 reports where occurcountry is known, 120,528 (60.3% of the full sample, 67.6% of known-country reports) describe an event that happened in the United States. The next-largest origin countries are Canada (10,235, 5.1%), the United Kingdom (7,048, 3.5%), Japan (6,573, 3.3%), and France (6,564, 3.3%). Germany (1.7%), China (1.6%), Italy (1.3%), and Spain (1.0%) round out the top of the international tail. This is a classic FAERS pattern: a heavy US plurality with substantial reporting from major pharmaceutical markets, mostly funneled through manufacturers' international pharmacovigilance offices.

data_table.description: Top 15 occur-countries (where the adverse event happened)

ana_27.label: Reporter country and event country agree 99.9% of the time
ana_27.content: When both occurcountry and primarysourcecountry are present (177,520 reports), they match in 177,310 (99.9%). The slight US bias toward the reporter side — 68.4% of reports filed from the US versus 60.3% of events in the US — comes from reports where occurcountry is blank but the reporter is US-based. In practice, this means FAERS does not capture cases where US clinicians forward reports about events in other countries; the system is filtered through reporters who are local to the patient.

matching: 177,310 (99.88%)
reports filed FROM US: 136,887 (68.44%)

ana_28.label: Four of every five reports come in through spontaneous MedWatch-style channels
ana_28.content: The reporttype field tells us where reports come from: 80.7% are Spontaneous (code 1) — the canonical MedWatch consumer/clinician submissions plus manufacturer-mandated spontaneous forwarding. 16.4% are tagged 'Report from study' (code 2), meaning they originate from clinical trials or observational studies that manufacturers run on already-approved drugs. The remaining 2.8% are 'Other' (code 3), typically literature reports or solicited safety surveys. Only 210 reports (0.1%) lack a reporttype value. The Study channel is small numerically but carries disproportionately high seriousness — it includes oncology trial safety reports.

data_table.description: Report-type breakdown

ana_29.label: Daily volume reveals a hard weekday/weekend bureaucracy
ana_29.content: Across the 54-day window, daily report counts oscillate wildly: weekdays average around 4,000–6,800 reports per day, while Saturdays and Sundays plummet to 400–900. January 6 (a Saturday) received 668 reports, January 7 (Sunday) received 464 — both less than 10% of the surrounding Friday's 6,621. The pattern repeats every weekend across both January and February. This is not because adverse events stop happening on weekends — it is because the reporting channels (manufacturer pharmacovigilance teams, FDA intake systems, hospital safety officers) work weekday shifts and queue weekend reports for Monday processing.

data_table.description: Daily report volume across the 54-day sampling window

ana_30.label: Weekdays carry 93% of all reports
ana_30.content: Aggregating by day-of-week across the eight weeks of the window, weekdays total 186,244 reports (93.1% of all 200,000) while Saturdays and Sundays combined total just 13,756 (6.9%). The most active day is Wednesday (39,720 reports), the least active is Saturday (5,561). The asymmetry — Sunday (8,195) is higher than Saturday (5,561) — likely reflects manufacturers queuing weekend reports for early-Monday submission, with some of those submissions being timestamped to Sunday because of overnight batch processing.

ana_32.label: GLP-1 head-to-head: same class, very different report profiles
ana_32.content: Restricting to suspect-role reports for the eight major GLP-1 brand names, the brands split sharply on seriousness despite covering similar therapeutic territory. Mounjaro (3,159 suspect-reports, 11.0% serious, 0.70% death) and Zepbound (718 reports, 2.5% serious, 0.0% death) — both tirzepatide products — are remarkably mild compared with Ozempic (2,493 reports, 32.0% serious, 0.6% death) and Rybelsus (260, 35.8% serious, 1.2% death), both semaglutide. Wegovy (semaglutide for weight loss) sits in between at 25.0% serious. Saxenda (liraglutide for weight loss) is an outlier at 90.5% serious, but the sample is small (63 reports). Female share is high across all brands (60–82%); US share is even higher (80–98%); median age is younger for the weight-loss-indicated brands (Wegovy 47, Zepbound 49, Saxenda 45.5) than for the diabetes-indicated brands (Ozempic 63, Rybelsus 63, Trulicity 63).

data_table.description: GLP-1 brand head-to-head: report count, seriousness, demographics (suspect role only)

notable_instance.name: Zepbound's 2.5% serious rate
notable_instance.value: Of 718 suspect-reports, just 18 are tagged serious and zero involve a death
notable_instance.why: Zepbound (tirzepatide approved for weight loss in Nov 2023) had the mildest reported safety profile of any major drug in the sample — a striking contrast to its identical-active-ingredient sibling Mounjaro's tougher reports.

ana_33.label: Mounjaro's complaints are about the pen; Ozempic's are about the body
ana_33.content: The top reactions for the two leading GLP-1 brands look almost like reports from different drugs. Mounjaro's top complaints are dosing-and-device events: 'Incorrect dose administered' (21.7% of Mounjaro reports), 'Injection site pain' (14.5%), 'Off label use' (12.5%), 'Extra dose administered' (7.7%), 'Injection site haemorrhage' (6.9%). Only at rank 4 does a biological symptom appear ('Nausea', 9.9%). Ozempic's profile is the inverse: 'Nausea' is #1 (16.2%), followed by 'Off label use' (10.1%), 'Vomiting' (9.3%), 'Diarrhoea' (9.2%), 'Constipation' (7.6%), and 'Decreased appetite' (6.8%). Most plausibly, the two drugs use different pen-injector devices and have different reporter communities — Mounjaro's pen seems to invite more device-handling complaints, while Ozempic's older clinical-trial reporting habits leak through into more symptom-style reports.

ana_34.label: What GLP-1 reports actually say: hunger, gastroparesis, dose mishaps
ana_34.content: Computing each reaction's representation rate inside GLP-1 reports versus the whole dataset reveals a class signature. The most over-represented reactions are 'Allodynia' (21.2x more common in GLP-1 reports than in the dataset average), 'Weight loss poor' (18.5x — patients reporting the drug isn't taking enough weight off), 'Impaired gastric emptying' (14.8x — the gastroparesis signal that became a 2024 news story), 'Eructation' (13.9x — burping), 'Accidental underdose' (13.6x), 'Hunger' (12.4x), 'Increased appetite' (11.1x), 'Pancreatitis' (8.4x — a long-known GLP-1 risk), 'Incorrect dose administered' (8.2x), and 'Injection site pain' (5.4x). The paradox at the heart of the class is on display: both 'Weight loss poor' AND 'Increased appetite' show extreme lift, alongside 'Hunger' — meaning a non-trivial subset of reports are from patients complaining the drug isn't working as advertised.

caveats.content: Time window: this sample covers Jan 1 – Feb 23, 2024 only — the first 54 days of the year. Any 'trend' is a within-window trend, not an annual or seasonal one. The full 2024 universe is ~1.32 million reports of which this sample is ~15%.

FAERS has no denominator. A report count cannot be divided by the number of people taking the drug, so 'Mounjaro outranks Ozempic 3:1' means 'three times more reports' — not 'three times more dangerous per prescription'.
Reporting bias and notoriety bias are large. Recent press coverage and regulatory warnings (e.g. the Ozempic/GLP-1 news in 2023–2024) measurably increase reporting for affected drugs.
Drug-name normalization is approximate. The dataset contains 16,877 distinct normalized drug names; we matched GLP-1 brands by pattern, which may miss compounded or unbranded mentions.

Death/seriousness sub-flag encoding in the supplied CSV is 1=yes, 2=no, NaN=missing. The README states 1=yes, blank=no — that is incorrect for this file. Every seriousness statistic here counts the value 1.

Reactions and seriousness are correlated with reporter community, not just drug pharmacology. The Mounjaro vs Ozempic seriousness gap likely reflects who is filing reports as much as what the drugs are doing.
